The financial

PART 1 – KEY INFORMATION

PURPOSE OF THE REPORT

To present to Cabinet the Housing Competence and Conduct Policy for consideration and adoption.


EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This report presents the Housing Competence and Conduct Policy for adoption. The policy builds on
the strong services already delivered by housing staff and provides a consistent framework to ensure
that employees and relevant service providers have the knowledge, skills, experience and behaviours
needed to deliver high-quality landlord services. The policy embeds the Chartered Institute of Housing
Professional Standards and a Housing Code of Conduct for Staff.

The policy will support the development of a competent and professional workforce that supports
better decisions and more consistent services; this improves tenants’ experience and outcomes; and
effective governance and evidence provide assurance that standards are being maintained.

The policy covers workforce planning, recruitment, induction, learning and development, professional
qualifications, appraisal, performance management and tenant oversight. Tenant feedback has been
incorporated into the final version of the policy, with being treated respectfully, being listened to,
receiving an empathetic response and being kept informed identified as the key themes. The full
tenant feedback on the policy is available on the Council’s website. The Code of Conduct that is
appended to the policy is subject to tenant scrutiny and feedback. Consultation closes on the 28
October 2026 and any feedback received will be incorporated into the policy in line with the delegated
powers referred to in Recommendation 2 (below).

The policy also supports compliance with the Regulator of Social Housing’s Competence and Conduct
Standard and associated qualification requirements. Implementation will be monitored through the
Competence and Conduct Action Plan, providing assurance that development needs are addressed,
professional standards are maintained and conti

2) Delegates authority to the Corporate Director for Operations and Delivery to make future
 updates or amendments to the policy in consultation with the Portfolio Holder responsible
 for Housing. The policy will be reviewed annually during implementation of the Competence
 and Conduct Action Plan and no later than October 2027, unless earlier review is required in
 response to tenant feedback.




REASON(S) FOR THE RECOMMENDATION(S)

The recommendations ensure that the policy is appropriately adopted in accordance with the Council’s
Constitution and provide evidence that the Council has a clear, accountable framework for meeting the
Competence and Conduct Standard and associated qualification requirements.




ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED

The alternative would be not to adopt a specific Housing Competence and Conduct Policy and to rely
on existing corporate employment and learning arrangements. This option is not recommended because
the Regulator of Social Housing’s Competence and Conduct Standard requires registered providers to
have a written policy covering the management and development of relevant staff, learning and
development, appraisal and performance management, and the steps taken in relation to relevant staff
employed by service providers.

Failure to meet the Standard could expose the Council to regulatory scrutiny and enforcement action,
while also increasing operational risks arising from inconsistent practice, skills gaps, inadequate
oversight and conduct that does not meet the expectations of tenants or the Council.

Without a consolidated and published policy, responsibilities and evidence requirements would be less
clear, making consistent implementation, tenant scrutiny and assurance more difficult. Adoption is
therefore the most appropriate option.

The policy contributes to a number of Corporate Plan 2024-28 themes:

  Financial sustainability and openness

The Cabinet is
asked to note any announcements made by Members of the Cabinet.
Minutes:
Connect
Tendring
The Portfolio
Holder for Arts, Culture & Heritage (Councillor Scott) made the
following statement:-
“Earlier this year,
we launched ‘Connect Tendring - Where Culture and Community
Meet’, a new creative and cultural newsletter designed to
connect artists, organisations, educators and residents with
opportunities across the district. I am pleased to report that it
already has around 450 subscribers. The latest edition was
distributed this week and included highlights from Arts Council
England's recent visit to Tendring, a call for artists to respond
to exciting public art opportunities on the seafront micro venue,
information on wider funding opportunities, updates from the
Creative Teachers Network, and details of Arts Council England's
new National Portfolio Investment Programme for 2028 to 2033.
Following their visit to
Tendring, Arts Council England highlighted that National Lottery
Project Grants investment in Tendring has increased six-fold, from
£85,000 in 2020/21 to more than £505,000 in 2025/26,
which alongside the launch of Creative Tendring, represents a
significant achievement and demonstrates the growing strength of
our creative sector and the impact of partnership working across
the district.
I would like to encourage
fellow Councillors to sign up to Connect Tendring. If you would
like to receive future editions, you can do so via the newsletter
sign up page on the Tendring District Council website. This growing
engagement is a real positive for Tendring, and I look forward to

The Cabinet considered a report of the
Executive Director (Environment and Place) which sought agreement
to comply with the Government’s direction by publishing the
Southend Regulation 19 Proposed Submission (draft) Local Plan for a
minimum six-week consultation period, to enable representations on

In accordance with Cabinet Procedure Rules

provided. A copy of the questions and responses were published on
the Council’s website alongside the minutes.
Reason(s) for decision
National policy requires every local council
to maintain an up-to-date local plan, which provides the framework
for planning decisions in its area. A local plan can
‘allocate’ sites for development and set policies that
guide how new development is shaped, managed and delivered, while
protecting the fabric of the local area.
Having an adopted up-to-date local plan helps
ensure development is of the right type, in the right location and
supported by the required infrastructure. Without a local plan,
development would not stop but is much more likely to come forward
in an un-coordinated and ‘speculative’ way, with less
supporting infrastructure, and fewer benefits and protections for
existing residents. The existing Development Plan is now out of
date and does not reflect significant social, environmental and
economic changes or how the market has responded. New up to date
criteria-based policies will allow a much more robust and evidenced
approach to the management of planning applications, including for
example Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs), affordable housing,
and hot food takeaways.
The recommendations set out in this report are
intended to help ensure the expeditious and legally robust
production of a new Local Plan for Southend. The Local Plan will
ensure the Council has strong local control of decision making and
will continue to be able to make planning decisions, aligned to a

Minutes:
Officers advised the report provides an update
on Thurrock's implementation of the Families First Partnership
Programme (FFPP), Transformation in the Service and the Kinship
Zones Pilot and sets out progress made to date, key developments
underway and priorities for delivery during 2026/27.
Members were advised that the
programme sought to shift the focus of services towards earlier
intervention and prevention, ensuring that families received
support at the earliest opportunity. The reform programme aimed to
provide whole-family support through stronger partnership working
across agencies, strengthen safeguarding arrangements, and reduce
the number of children entering care where safe and appropriate
alternatives could be identified.
The Committee was informed
that Thurrock had been selected as one of seven national Kinship
Zones pilot authorities. Members heard that the pilot sought to
promote and strengthen kinship care arrangements by supporting
children to remain safely within their wider family networks
wherever possible.
The programme would provide
practical, emotional and financial support to kinship carers,
reduce the need for care proceedings, and improve long-term
outcomes for children by maintaining family connections and
stability.
Officers outlined progress
made to date in implementing the reforms.
Members were advised that ten
Family Help Teams had been established to provide integrated
support to families and improve coordination between services. A
single assessment and planning framework had also been introduced
to ensure a more consistent and streamlined approach to identifying
needs and delivering interventions.
The Committee heard that work
was progressing on the development of a Multi-Agency Child
Protection Team (MACPT), bringing together professionals from a
range of partner organisations to strengthen information sharing,
joint decision-making and safeguarding practice. Members were also
informed that Family Network Meetings were being utilised more
frequently to identify support available within extended family
networks and to enable families to play a greater role in planning
for children's needs.
Officers further advised that
specialist practitioner roles had been expanded to strengthen
professional expertise and improve support for children and
families with more complex needs. Ongoing workforce development
activity was also taking place, including training programmes and
partnership development work, to ensure staff and partner agencies
were equipped to deliver the new operating model
effectively.
Members discussed how success
would be measured. Officers advised that key indicators would
include reductions in the number of children entering care,
increases in successful reunification with families, and improved
outcomes when benchmarked against statistical
neighbours.
The Committee sought
information regarding the effectiveness of the Kinship Zones Pilot.
Officers advised that the programme remained in its early stages,
having commenced in April 2026, and that it was too early to draw
definitive conclusions. However, success would ultimately be
measured by reductions in care numbers and increased support for
children remaining safely within their family networks.
Members expressed support for

be beneficial. Officers responded that supporting children within

significant potential for improved outcomes where appropriate
support mechanisms were available.

items.title: Update on progress to address Regulator of Social Housing Judgement
items.text:
Report of the Executive
Director for Environment and Place
Minutes:
The Committee received a report
updating Members on progress made in addressing matters arising
from the Regulator of Social Housing judgement together with
ongoing engagement with the Housing Ombudsman and Building Safety
Regulator.
The Head of Housing advised
that monthly meetings continued with the Regulator of Social
Housing and that significant progress had been made against a
number of actions within the Provider Improvement Plan. Members
were informed that the Council had achieved 100% communal
Electrical Installation Condition Report (EICR) coverage and 99%
domestic EICR coverage. It was reported that electrical safety was
now considered by the Regulator to be a business-as-usual activity.
Significant improvements had also been achieved in relation to
stock condition surveys and tenant equality, diversity and
inclusion data.
The Committee was advised that
repairs performance remained an area of focus. Whilst improvements
had been achieved, a targeted improvement plan had been agreed with
the Council's repairs contractor to reduce work in progress and
improve performance to industry norms by Christmas 2026.
Members were informed that the
Housing Ombudsman's investigation had concluded, with the Ombudsman
acknowledging the Council's understanding of the issues identified
and the actions being taken to address them. A learning statement
would be submitted to the Ombudsman as the final stage of the
process.
In relation to building safety,
officers reported that further building safety cases had been
requested by the Building Safety Regulator and that the Council
continued to meet statutory deadlines and respond to regulatory
requirements.
During discussion, Members
sought clarification regarding the frequency of regulatory
inspections, the role of the various regulatory bodies and whether
issues identified had come as a surprise to officers. Officers
explained that this was the first inspection under the new consumer
regulation framework and advised that the Council was aware of
areas requiring improvement before the inspections took
place.
Members questioned officers
regarding repairs performance, contractor management arrangements
and potential consequences should performance improvements not be
achieved. Officers advised that detailed performance improvement
plans were in place and were being monitored closely.
The Committee requested that a
further update on repairs performance be brought back to a future
meeting in January 2027.
Members welcomed the progress
achieved in relation to electrical safety, stock condition surveys
and tenant equality, diversity and inclusion data. It was further
suggested that meetings of the South Essex Homes Board should be
publicised more widely to elected Members.
Resolved:
1.
That the continued work underway with the Regulator
of Social Housing be endorsed.
2.
That the conclusion of the Housing Ombudsman's
investigation be noted.
3.
That the current position regarding Building Safety
Regulator requirements be noted and the ongoing work towards
compliance be endorsed.

majority of recorded incidents continued to arise from human error

phishing exercises, penetration testing and compliance with
government cyber standards.
Members also considered the
increasing use of artificial intelligence within the Council.

areas, including administration, minute-taking and information
management, and that governance arrangements had been established
to ensure its safe and appropriate use.

data-sharing requirements.
Members welcomed the positive

environment.

HUMAN RESOURCES & COUNCIL TAX COMMITTEE

 22 OCTOBER 2026

 REPORT OF DIRECTOR OF PEOPLE

A.1 RETIREMENT AND FLEXIBLE RETIREMENT POLICY

PART 1 – KEY INFORMATION

PURPOSE OF THE REPORT
The purpose of this report is to seek the Human Resources and Council Tax Committee’s approval of
the revised Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy at Appendix A, which establishes a clear and
consistent process for retirement and flexible retirement applications.


EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The revised Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy establishes a single, clear and consistent
framework for the management of standard and flexible retirement arrangements. It confirms that the
Council does not operate a compulsory retirement age and reflects the relevant requirements of
employment and equality legislation and the Local Government Pension Scheme (LGPS).

The principal provisions of the revised Policy are as follows:

  Introduction of a standard Retirement/Flexible Retirement Notification Form, with employees
 expected, wherever possible, to provide at least three months’ written notice.
  A five-stage process covering early discussion, the provision of pension information, formal
 notification, confirmation of arrangements and completion of the Council’s leaver process.
  A requirement for employees to obtain appropriate pension information and consider the financial
 implications before making a final decision, recognising that the Council is unable to provide
 financial advice.
  Eligibility criteria for flexible retirement, which may be available to eligible permanent employees
 who are active LGPS members and have reached the applicable normal minimum pension age,
 subject to a permanent reduction in contractual hours of more than 25%, a reduction of at least
 one grade, or both.
  Consideration of each flexible retirement application on its individual merits, having regard to
 business continuity, service provision, operational impact, affordability, workforce and
 succession planning, recruitment implications, knowledge retention and any relevant precedent.
  Consideration of the application by the relevant Corporate Director, followed by submission to
 the Workfor

[page 2]
LGPS to build up further benefits, including through the 50/50 section where appropriate. Where an
application is refused, the employee may use the Council’s Grievance Appeals Procedure.

Implementation of the revised Policy will provide a clear and consistently administered route through
retirement and flexible retirement. The proposed notice and notification arrangements will allow
sufficient time for Essex Pension Fund and the Council’s Payroll and Payments Team to obtain
estimates and complete the necessary pension and employment processes.

The revised arrangements will support business continuity, service provision and effective workforce
and succession planning. They will also facilitate knowledge transfer and the retention of skills and
experience where operationally appropriate, while promoting fair, transparent and consistent decision-
making across Council services.

The Policy also defines the respective responsibilities of employees, managers, the People Team and
the Payroll and Payments Team, thereby strengthening compliance with employment, equality and
LGPS requirements and reducing procedural and financial risk.


RECOMMENDATION(S)
It is recommended that the Human Resources & Council Tax Committee:

a) approves the Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy attached at Appendix A;

b) subject to a) above, notes that flexible retirement applications will be considered in
line with the approved Policy and determined in accordance with the delegations set out
in the Council’s Constitution; and

c) authorises the Director of People to implement the approved Policy and, in
accordance with the Council’s delegated arrangements, make any minor, consequential
or legislative amendments to associated procedures, guidance and documentation that
do not materially alter the Policy.


REASON(S) FOR THE RECOMMENDATION(S)
The revised Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy introduces a standard application form for both
retirement and flexible retirement, providing employees with a clear and consistent process to follow.

This will reduce the risk of insufficient notice being given and help ensure that the Essex Pension Fund
has adequate time to process pension

[page 3]
ALTERNATIVE OPTIONS CONSIDERED
Employees seeking access to their Local Government Pension Scheme (LGPS) benefits, whether
through retirement from the Council or as part of a flexible retirement arrangement, must follow the
relevant LGPS requirements. Essex Pension Fund has requested that employees provide at least three
months’ notice of their intention to retire. This allows sufficient time for pension benefits to be processed
and made available from the intended retirement date. Where insufficient notice is given, an employee
may retire from their post before their pension benefits become payable, potentially placing them in a
difficult financial position.

The Policy is intended to reduce this financial risk by promoting timely notification. It will also provide
managers with additional time to plan for any vacancy or change in service capacity arising from an
employee’s departure or reduction in working hours.


PART 2 – IMPLICATIONS OF THE DECISION

DELIVERING PRIORITIES
The revised Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy supports the Council’s Corporate Plan 2024–
2028, principally the themes of Pride in our area and services to residents and Financial
sustainability and openness.

Pride in our area and services to residents: timely and consistent retirement planning supports
continuity and resilience across Council services. It enables services to plan proactively for vacancies
and changes in working arrangements, retain organisational knowledge where appropriate and maintain
reliable service delivery for residents.

Financial sustainability and openness: the Policy provides a transparent and consistently applied
framework for managing retirement and flexible retirement requests. It supports effective workforce and
succession planning, informed management of organisational capacity and appropriate control of
financial implications, including the normal expectation that flexible retirement will not create additional
pension strain costs for the Council.

LEGAL REQUIREMENTS (including legislation & constitutional powers)
The revised Policy has been developed having regard to the Equality Act 2010, the Employment Rights
Act 1996, the Local Government Pensi

[page 4]
The Regulations govern pension benefits and entitlements for eligible Council employees. Flexible
retirement requires the Council’s consent and must be administered in accordance with the Regulations
and the Council’s approved pension discretions.

The Human Resources and Council Tax Committee has responsibility for approving the Retirement and
Flexible Retirement Policy in accordance with the Council’s Constitution. Under Part 3 of the
Constitution, the relevant Corporate Director has delegated authority to act on staff-management
matters within their area of responsibility. The Corporate Director will consider an individual flexible
retirement application before submitting it to the Workforce Panel, comprising the Section 151 Officer
and the Head of People. The Panel may endorse the application but has no delegated decision-making
powers. The formal decision will therefore be taken by the relevant Corporate Director, having regard to
the Panel’s advice. Ian Davidson, as Chief Executive and Head of Paid Service, holds delegated
authority in relation to regrading posts, restructuring and determining staffing levels. Any application
engaging those delegations, or falling outside the approved Policy, must be referred to the Head of Paid
Service or determined through the appropriate constitutional route.

FINANCE AND OTHER RESOURCE IMPLICATIONS
The implementation of the Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy does not create significant
additional financial implications.

Effective retirement planning enables:

  Better workforce planning.
  Reduced business disruption.
  Improved succession planning.
  Retention of knowledge and expertise through flexible retirement, where appropriate.

The Policy also reinforces the Council's existing requirement that flexible retirement arrangements
should not create additional pension strain costs for the Council unless exceptionally approved.

defined as best value authorities in Part 1 of the Local Government Act 1999 (“the 1999 Act”) to “make
arrangements to secure continuous impro

 their workforce.

MILESTONES AND DELIVERY
The adoption and implementation of the Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy will follow the
timeline below:

  Management Team – 6 October 2026
  Human Resources and Council Tax Committee – 22 October 2026

Following formal approval, the Policy will be shared with managers across the organisation to promote
a consistent and robust approach to retirement planning for employees.

ASSOCIATED RISKS AND MITIGATION
The introduction of the revised Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy will help manage and mitigate
a range of organisational risks, including workforce planning gaps, loss of organisational knowledge,
inconsistent management practices, delayed pension applications, age discrimination claims and non-
compliance with employment and pension regulations.

OUTCOME OF CONSULTATION AND ENGAGEMENT
The local union branch executive was consulted on the proposed revisions to the Council’s Retirement
and Flexible Retirement Policy, and its feedback was considered in developing the revised Policy. The
revised procedure will also be communicated to managers to support consistent application and timely
decision-making.

In addition, advice and input have been sought from the Council’s Payroll, Payments and Business
Manager regarding compliance with the LGPS application process.


EQUALITIES
Section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 establishes the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED). The revised
Retirement and Flexible Retirement Policy supports the Council's commitment to equality by:

 (a) Confirming that the Council does not operate a compulsory retirement age.

The protected characteristics under the Act are: age, disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy and

items.title: Career Track - Verbal Update
items.text:
The Committee will
receive an oral update regarding the Council’s Career Track
service.
Minutes:
The Work Based
Learning Manager provided a verbal update on the Career Track
apprenticeship programme. It was reported that there were currently
53 active apprentices enrolled on the programme, of whom 25 were
employed by Tendring District Council. Members were advised that
one in five current Council employees were either current or former
Career Track apprentices.
The programme
continued to successfully attract young people, with 26% of
apprentices aged 16 to 18 and 60% aged 19 to 24.
It was further
reported that the programme was delivered in partnership with a
number of local authorities, including Colchester City Council,
Braintree District Council, Maldon District Council, Suffolk County
Council, Kent County Council and the London Borough of Hounslow.
Apprenticeships currently offered included Level 2 and Level 3
qualifications in Customer Service, Business Administration and
Public Service Operational Delivery Officer, with a new Level 2
Administration Assistant apprenticeship having been introduced in
August 2026.
Dedicated funding
for Career Track had been included within the 2026/27 budget,
resulting in 17 new apprentice starts during the year, with a
further six apprentices expected to commence shortly.
Members noted that
apprentices had been recruited across a range of service areas,
including the People Team, People Development’ Leisure
Centres, Parking, Information Technology, the Contact Centre, the
Print Unit, Governance, Elections and Housing
Solutions/Compliance.
The Work Based
Learning Manager advised that the programme continued to perform
strongly, maintaining a 95% success rate for the 2025/26 academic
year and retaining its Ofsted rating of "Good".
The Chairman
requested that a report on the 3-year funding received for the
Career Track programme be submitted to the Committee's programmed
meeting on 8 July 2027, in order that a follow-up review could be
undertaken.
The Chairman of the
Committee read out the following statement:-
“The Committee has
consistently recognised the value of Career Track and the important
contribution it makes to developing local talent, creating
opportunities and supporting the Council’s future
workforce.
I would also like, on
behalf of the Committee, to place on record our sincere thanks to
the Leader of the Council and the Chief Executive for their
continued support for Career Track. When this Committee asked for
their support in advocating for the continuation and future
development of the programme, they responded extremely positively,
and we are very grateful for their continued commitment.
It is particularly
encouraging to see the wider support and investment that Career
Track has received across the Council, enabling the programme to
grow and create more opportunities for local people to develop
their skills and careers, while also supporting the development and
progression of our existing workforce. The Committee very much
welcomes this and is proud to continue championing Career Track and
the opportunities it provides.”
The Committee noted
the foregoing.

environmental crime through enforcement action, investigation and

illegally dumping waste. The Council currently has the ability to

ultimately borne by law-abiding residents.

photographs, CCTV or dashcam evidence where available, enabling the

PURPOSE OF THE REPORT

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Tendring’s Heritage Strategy (2020) identified the preparation and adoption of updated
Conservation Area Character Appraisals and Management Plans for all 20 conservation areas
within the District as a key priority, including the five conservation areas identified on Historic
England’s Heritage at Risk Register.

This report presents the final two appraisals and management plans within that programme,
covering St Osyth and Manningtree & Mistley. Both documents have been prepared and refined
through extensive engagement with local communities and stakeholders, including a series of
public consultations undertaken between 2022 and 2026. Consultation responses have
informed revisions to the appraisal documents and, where appropriate, proposed changes to
the conservation area boundaries.

The updated appraisals provide an evidence-based assessment of the significance, character
and appearance of the conservation areas and identify opportunities to preserve and enhance
their special interest. Once adopted, they will become material planning considerations, helping
to inform planning decisions and guide future management of these important heritage assets.

To progress projects specifically identified in the Council’s Heritage Strategy.

Conservation Area Character Appraisals and Management Plans as a material consideration
in planning decisions. The Council’s ability to conserve and enhance the District’s historic
environment would be reduced.

Having up-to-date Conservation Area Character Appraisals and Management Plans will assist

within the Corporate Plan (Our Vision) 2024-2028. Following consultation on Issues and

the Local Plan for a final six-week consultation prior to its submission for independent
examination.

The proposed adoption of the St Osyth and Manningtree & Mistley Conservation Area
Character Appraisals and Management Plans also supports a number of wider priorities within
the Corporate Plan. By identifying and celebrating the special historic and architectural interest
of these areas, the documents contribute towards the priority of promoting our heritage offer,
attracting visitors and encouraging them to stay longer. They also support championing our
local environment by providing a framework for preserving and enhancing the District's historic
built environment and local distinctiveness.
